questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines hybrid identity, as Lesson 1 describes it?
options: A single identity that originates in on-prem Active Directory and is also recognized by cloud identity services, instead of existing as two separate, disconnected accounts
Two separate accounts, one on-prem and one in the cloud, manually kept in sync by IT whenever something changes
A cloud-only identity that replaces on-prem Active Directory entirely once an organization adopts Microsoft 365
An on-prem-only identity that cloud services are configured to ignore, so users sign into cloud apps with a completely different account
A temporary identity used only during the migration period before an organization switches fully to the cloud
A shared generic account that every employee uses to sign into both on-prem and cloud resources
questions.explain: Hybrid identity means one identity recognized in both places: the user object lives in on-prem AD, is synchronized into Entra ID, and the organization makes one deliberate decision about how sign-in is verified. It is specifically the alternative to the two-separate-logins problem the 800-employee manufacturing example in Lesson 1 describes.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is exactly the painful manual-dual-account scenario Lesson 1 uses to show why hybrid identity is necessary in the first place — two separate logins, two separate passwords, and IT having to disable both accounts separately on offboarding. Hybrid identity exists precisely to eliminate that setup, not to describe it.

questions.prompt: An admin just updated a user's group membership in on-prem AD and doesn't want to wait up to 30 minutes for the next scheduled run. Per Lesson 2, which cmdlet forces that specific change to sync immediately?
options: Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
Get-ADSyncScheduler
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Full
questions.explain: A delta sync only picks up what changed since the last cycle, which is exactly what's needed right after a single group-membership change. Initial forces a full re-import of everything in scope, which is unnecessary overhead here; Get-ADSyncScheduler only displays the current schedule without triggering anything; -PolicyType Full isn't one of the options Lesson 2 names.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Password Hash Sync, Federation, and Pass-Through Authentication, per Lesson 3.
options: Password Hash Sync keeps cloud sign-in working even if the on-prem network goes down, because the hash was already synced ahead of time
Federation redirects the sign-in to an on-prem AD FS server, so the password or its hash never reaches Entra ID
Pass-Through Authentication stores a password hash in the cloud, the same way Password Hash Sync does
Password Hash Sync is the default authentication method Microsoft Entra Connect uses
Federation requires no additional servers beyond what Password Hash Sync needs
questions.explain: PHS syncs an already-hashed value ahead of time, so cloud sign-in keeps working even if on-prem goes down, and it's Entra Connect's default. Federation redirects the browser to an on-prem AD FS server so the password or hash never touches Entra ID at all. Pass-Through Authentication is the opposite of option C's claim — it validates the password against AD in real time and never stores a hash in the cloud. Federation also requires building and maintaining an AD FS server farm, which is real extra infrastructure PHS doesn't need.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in AWS IAM Identity Center, a ________ is a named collection of IAM permissions that an administrator assigns to a user or group for a specific AWS account.
questions.explain: A permission set is how IAM Identity Center grants access without ever creating separate IAM credentials in each account — administrators assign users or groups to accounts with a specific permission set, all managed centrally from one place.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the castle-and-moat model from Zero Trust, per Lesson 5?
options: Castle-and-moat grants implicit trust to anything already inside the network perimeter; Zero Trust verifies every request explicitly regardless of network location
Zero Trust grants implicit trust to anything already inside the network perimeter; castle-and-moat verifies every request explicitly regardless of network location
Castle-and-moat and Zero Trust both ignore network location entirely and rely only on device health
Zero Trust is simply castle-and-moat with a stronger firewall placed at the network edge
Castle-and-moat requires MFA on every single request, while Zero Trust only requires MFA once at initial sign-in
The two models are functionally identical; only the marketing name changed
questions.explain: Castle-and-moat built a strong perimeter and then trusted anything already inside it, which worked only as long as there was a clear physical network edge to defend. Zero Trust is the response to that edge disappearing: every request is verified explicitly, every time, using real signals about who is asking — location is one signal among several, never by itself a reason to skip verification.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two models' mechanics entirely backwards — it's castle-and-moat that grants blanket implicit trust to anything already inside the perimeter, and Zero Trust that insists on explicit verification regardless of where a request comes from. Reversing which model does the trusting and which does the verifying is exactly the mix-up this lesson is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each Zero Trust networking term from Lesson 6 to what it actually means.
right: An attacker moving from one compromised system to others on the same network
A rule design where no traffic is permitted between segments unless a rule explicitly allows it
Breaking a network into many small, individually secured segments instead of one large trusted zone
Traffic moving between systems inside a network, as opposed to traffic entering or leaving it
questions.explain: Microsegmentation is the design of breaking one large trusted zone into many small, individually secured segments. Lateral movement is exactly what that design is meant to contain — an attacker spreading from one compromised workload to others. East-west traffic is the industry term for traffic moving between internal systems, which microsegmentation now scrutinizes the way a firewall once scrutinized only the network's edge. Deny-by-default is the rule posture that makes all of this work: nothing is permitted between segments unless a rule explicitly says so.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Zero Trust's tenets and Conditional Access, per Lessons 5 and 8.
options: Zero Trust's three tenets are verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach
A Conditional Access policy evaluates its conditions once at initial sign-in and does not re-check them for the rest of the session
Requiring a compliant device before granting access is an example of least privilege access in practice
Treating an unfamiliar sign-in location as a trigger for re-verification is an example of the assume breach tenet in practice
Network location is completely ignored under Zero Trust and carries no weight as a signal at all
questions.explain: Zero Trust rests on verify explicitly, least privilege access, and assume breach. Conditional Access is explicitly not a one-time gate — Entra ID re-evaluates its conditions on every single access attempt, which is the opposite of option B. Requiring a compliant device is least privilege in action (don't hand access to just any device), and treating an unfamiliar location as a trigger is assume breach in action (notice when something looks different rather than assuming nothing changed). Location isn't ignored entirely — it's one signal among several, just never by itself the deciding factor.

questions.prompt: A user signs in from a managed laptop that passes every check. Twenty minutes later, a required security update fails to install. Put these events from Lesson 8's example in the correct order.
items: User signs in from a managed laptop — MFA satisfied, device compliant, location trusted — access granted
A required security update fails to install, and the laptop's device-compliance check fails
The user's session tries to reach a protected resource again
Conditional Access re-evaluates its conditions and finds the device-compliance condition no longer holds
The next access attempt is challenged or blocked, without the user ever logging out and back in
questions.explain: This is continuous verification in action: the session passed every check at sign-in, a trust signal changed mid-session (the failed update), and the very next access attempt — not a new login — is where Conditional Access catches the change and reacts. Nothing here required the user to sign out first, which is exactly the point Lesson 8 is making about re-checking conditions on every attempt rather than once.

questions.prompt: An attacker obtains a valid but leaked access key to a storage account that has default encryption at rest (AES-256) enabled, exactly as Lesson 9 describes. What happens when the attacker uses that key to read the data?
options: The attacker reads the data in plain, readable form, because the platform decrypts it transparently for any authorized request
The attacker cannot read anything at all, because AES-256 blocks every request that isn't made from the original application
The attacker can read the data only if they also separately steal the encryption key directly from Key Vault or KMS
The storage service automatically detects the stolen key is being misused and re-encrypts the data a second time
questions.explain: Encryption at rest defends against physical access to underlying hardware, not against someone who already holds valid, authorized credentials. The cloud platform decrypts data transparently for any authorized request — that's what makes the data usable at all — so a leaked access key lets an attacker read it in plain form exactly as if they were the legitimate application.

questions.prompt: Match each key-management term from Lesson 10 to what it actually is.
right: Periodically replacing a key's underlying material on a schedule, without breaking apps that use it
A physical or virtual device that generates and stores keys so the raw key material never leaves it
AWS's service, scoped specifically to generating, storing, and controlling access to encryption keys
Microsoft's centralized service for storing and managing keys, secrets, and certificates together
questions.explain: Azure Key Vault covers keys, secrets, and certificates under one roof. AWS KMS keeps its scope narrower, on purpose, to just encryption keys. An HSM is the hardware-backed device both services rely on so raw key material never leaves it. Key rotation is one of the four core jobs both services perform: generate, store, rotate, and gate access.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: deliberately deleting a customer-managed key to instantly and irreversibly destroy access to everything it protects is sometimes called ________, per Lesson 11.
questions.explain: Crypto-shredding is the deliberate, useful side of the real risk a CMK carries: because nobody, not even the cloud provider, can bypass the key, deleting it is a legitimate way to instantly and irreversibly destroy access to the data it protected.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about customer-managed keys (CMKs) vs. platform-managed keys (PMKs), per Lesson 11.
options: A CMK lets you set a custom rotation schedule and see a detailed audit log of every encrypt/decrypt operation against it
Platform-managed keys are cryptographically weaker than customer-managed keys, since the two don't use the same underlying algorithm
If a CMK is deleted or access to it is lost, the data it protected becomes permanently, cryptographically unreadable
Some compliance frameworks specifically require customer-managed keys as documented proof the customer, not the vendor, controls access
A platform-managed key requires you to generate and import it yourself into Key Vault or KMS before it can be used
questions.explain: A CMK hands you rotation control, audit visibility, and revocation that a PMK doesn't offer. Losing or deleting a CMK makes its protected data permanently unreadable, with no recovery path. Compliance frameworks require CMKs for documented proof of customer control, not because PMKs are weaker — both rely on the same AES-256 underneath. A platform-managed key is the opposite of option E's claim: the provider generates and manages it with zero setup from you.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't deleting a hardcoded secret in a later Git commit actually fix the exposure, per Lesson 13?
options: The secret still sits in the repository's earlier commits, and anyone with read access to that history can pull the plain-text value out with git log and git show
Git automatically re-encrypts every deleted value, so the exposure is fixed but just takes a few minutes to propagate
Deleting a line from a file also deletes that same line from every previous commit in the repository's history
The secret is removed everywhere it was deployed, including CI/CD logs and container images, the moment the commit is pushed
GitHub's secret scanner automatically rotates any secret it detects, so the old value stops working on its own
A secret only becomes exposed once it's deleted; leaving it in place untouched is actually safer
questions.explain: Removing a hardcoded secret in a new commit only hides it from someone who isn't looking at history — the value is still sitting in every earlier commit, retrievable with ordinary commands like git log and git show. The only real fix is rotating the credential and rewriting history to purge it, which is disruptive and easy to get wrong.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C claims deleting a line removes it from every previous commit too, which is backwards from how version control works — each past commit is a frozen snapshot, so the secret remains fully intact and retrievable in every commit before the deletion, no matter what a later commit does.

questions.code:
# Pseudocode: no password anywhere in this code
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()          # uses the resource's managed identity
client = SecretClient(vault_url, credential)
connection_string = client.get_secret("prod-orders-db-connection").value
questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, what does this pattern eliminate that a hardcoded connection string (Lesson 13) could not avoid?
options: Any credential stored in the application's own code, config file, or container image — the app instead proves its identity to Key Vault at runtime using its Managed Identity
The need for Key Vault to store the secret at all, since the value now lives only in application memory
The need for an access policy on the vault, since Managed Identity bypasses every access-control check
The requirement that the secret ever be rotated, since Managed Identity keeps the same value valid forever
questions.explain: A Managed Identity lets the app ask Azure AD for a token proving it is that specific resource, present that token to Key Vault, and receive the secret directly in memory — nothing in the code, source control, or a container image ever contains the real value. That removes the hardcoding problem entirely rather than just hiding it better. The vault still requires an access policy deciding which identity can read the secret, and rotation is still a separate concern Lesson 16 covers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ of a leaked-but-undetected credential is the length of time it remains valid before rotation invalidates it — per Lesson 16, a credential rotated every 30 days has at most a 30-day one.
questions.explain: Rotation doesn't prevent a leak; it shrinks the window of usefulness a leaked-but-undetected credential has, so even a leak nobody catches in time runs out the clock on its own.

questions.prompt: Put AWS Secrets Manager's automatic rotation steps for a supported service like Amazon RDS, per Lesson 15, in the correct order.
items: Secrets Manager's managed rotation Lambda function generates a new password
The rotation Lambda updates that new password on the RDS instance itself
The rotation Lambda updates the stored secret value in Secrets Manager to match
The application fetches the current value from Secrets Manager at its next connection, never noticing rotation happened
questions.explain: Rotation has to update the actual database before it updates the stored record of what the password is, and only after both are in sync does anything change for the application — which simply keeps asking for the current value and is never aware rotation ran at all.

questions.prompt: A CSPM scan surfaces a finding: a security group allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. Per Lesson 20's remediation workflow, what is the correct next step immediately after the finding is surfaced?
options: Assign the finding to the team or owner actually positioned to fix it
Immediately re-scan the environment to confirm the finding is gone
Auto-remediate the finding with no further steps, regardless of who owns the resource
Lower the environment's compliance score to reflect the new finding, and take no further action
questions.explain: The remediation workflow runs surface, then assign, then fix, then re-scan in that order. A finding nobody owns never gets fixed, which is exactly why assignment comes immediately after surfacing — before any fix, automated or manual, and well before the confirming re-scan.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about common cloud misconfigurations CSPM tools catch, per Lesson 18.
options: A security group rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or 3389 opens administrative access to the entire internet, not just the organization's own network
An IAM policy can be syntactically valid and still be flagged as an excessive-permissions finding
A storage resource is only flagged as a public-access finding if something sensitive is actually stored inside it
MFA not being enforced on a privileged account is a common finding even though most providers support MFA
Encryption-at-rest findings never occur anymore, since AWS and Azure enable it by default on new resources
questions.explain: 0.0.0.0/0 means any IPv4 address on the internet, so a rule like that on port 22 or 3389 opens administrative access well beyond the organization's own network. A wildcard IAM policy can be perfectly valid syntax and still be flagged as excessive permissions. MFA gaps on privileged accounts remain a common, real finding despite wide MFA availability. A storage finding doesn't require anything sensitive to actually be inside — the setting itself is the finding — and encryption findings still occur when encryption is explicitly disabled or configured weaker than the required baseline.

questions.prompt: Match each posture-management term from Lesson 19 to what it actually is.
right: Defender for Cloud's percentage summarizing alignment with the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark
AWS's native threat-detection service, one of several whose findings feed into an aggregator
Azure's native CSPM and workload protection tool, which can also assess AWS and GCP accounts
An AWS service that aggregates findings from AWS's own security services and third-party tools into one scored view
questions.explain: Defender for Cloud is built as a CSPM engine first, scoring against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark and extending to AWS and GCP. Security Hub is built as an aggregation layer, pulling together findings from AWS's own specialized services like GuardDuty into one scored dashboard. GuardDuty is one of those specialized services, focused on threat detection. Secure Score is specifically Defender for Cloud's own percentage output.

questions.prompt: Put the CSPM scan cycle, per Lesson 17, in the correct order.
items: Discover every resource across the environment
Compare each resource against a recognized security baseline
Flag any resource that drifts from the baseline as a finding
Re-scan the whole cycle again on a schedule
questions.explain: A CSPM tool has to see everything before it can check anything, so discovery comes first, followed by comparing each resource against a baseline, flagging any drift as a finding, and then repeating the whole cycle on a schedule — because a setting that was safe yesterday can be flipped open today.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a site-to-site VPN is unnecessary because two VNets are already connected with VNet peering. Which statement correctly explains why peering doesn't solve the on-prem-to-cloud connectivity problem, per Lesson 21?
options: VNet peering connects two cloud networks over the provider's own backbone and never touches the internet; it has no path to an on-prem network that isn't in the cloud at all
VNet peering and site-to-site VPN are actually the same technology, just with different names in the Azure portal
VNet peering can connect an on-prem network to a VNet, but only if both ends use exactly the same IP address range
Site-to-site VPN is only needed when more than two VNets are involved; two VNets alone never need it
VNet peering requires an IPsec tunnel over the public internet, exactly like a site-to-site VPN does
Peering replaces the need for a VPN Gateway, Local Network Gateway, and Connection resource entirely
questions.explain: Site-to-site VPN exists specifically because one side of the connection — the on-prem network — isn't in the cloud, so there's no backbone to put it on. VNet peering connects two cloud networks to each other over Azure's or AWS's own backbone and never touches the internet at all, which is exactly why it can't reach an on-prem office no matter how many VNets are peered together.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E claims peering needs the same IPsec tunnel over the public internet that a site-to-site VPN does, which is backwards — peering specifically avoids both the public internet and any encrypted tunnel by riding the provider's own backbone. It's the site-to-site VPN that needs IPsec over the internet, precisely because the on-prem side has no backbone connection to use instead.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic chain wants to send nightly, non-urgent backup data to the cloud with no compliance rule against the public internet. A payment processor wants a primary, always-on link carrying continuous transaction volume under PCI requirements. Per Lesson 23, which connection type fits each, and why?
options: The clinic fits site-to-site VPN (fast, cheap, and latency-tolerant); the payment processor fits a dedicated circuit (a compliance rule bars public-internet transit, and it's carrying primary production traffic at scale)
Both should use site-to-site VPN, since it's cheaper and traffic volume is the only factor that ever matters
Both should use ExpressRoute or Direct Connect, since any production traffic always requires a dedicated circuit
The clinic fits a dedicated circuit because backup data is always sensitive; the payment processor fits VPN because PCI has no requirement about public-internet transit
questions.explain: The clinic's nightly, non-urgent, non-regulated backup job is squarely VPN territory — fast, cheap, and the public-internet variability doesn't matter much as long as it finishes overnight. The payment processor's continuous, primary production traffic under PCI requirements is squarely dedicated-circuit territory, because a compliance rule against public-internet transit can't be satisfied by a VPN no matter how strong its encryption is — the traffic still technically crosses the internet underneath.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure ExpressRoute and AWS Direct Connect, per Lesson 22.
options: Traffic never touches the public internet at all, so there's no IPsec encryption layer because there's no shared public medium to encrypt against
A connectivity provider physically provisions the cross-connect at an ExpressRoute or Direct Connect location
These connections are typically faster to provision than a site-to-site VPN, often set up within hours
Azure's Private Peering reaches VNets, while Microsoft Peering reaches Microsoft 365 and other Microsoft services
A Direct Connect Gateway is used when one connection needs to reach VPCs in multiple regions
questions.explain: Because the traffic never enters the public internet, there's nothing for IPsec to encrypt against. A connectivity provider does the real physical work of the cross-connect. Private Peering and Microsoft Peering are the two real peering types Azure names for reaching VNets versus Microsoft 365. A Direct Connect Gateway extends one connection to multiple regions' VPCs. Provisioning is the opposite of option C's claim — it takes real lead time, often weeks, because of the physical cross-connect work involved, unlike a VPN's hours-long setup.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: both Azure and AWS provision a site-to-site VPN connection as ________ tunnels by default, each terminating on a different physical endpoint, so one can go down without taking the whole connection with it.
questions.explain: Two tunnels, each on a different physical endpoint inside the provider's infrastructure, is the default redundancy Lesson 21 describes — a single-tunnel VPN works for a lab, but production links rely on this failover so a maintenance event or hardware failure on one tunnel doesn't take the whole connection down.

questions.prompt: Why does a SOC 2 Type II report carry more weight with an enterprise buyer than a SOC 2 Type I report, per Lesson 26?
options: Type II tests whether controls actually operated effectively over a review period, typically six to twelve months, while Type I only evaluates whether controls were suitably designed at a single point in time
Type II is a pass/fail certificate, while Type I is only a self-reported checklist with no independent auditor involved
Type I covers all five Trust Services Criteria automatically, while Type II only ever covers Security
Type II reports are issued by ISO, while Type I reports are issued by the AICPA
questions.explain: A Type I report only evaluates whether controls were suitably designed at one point in time. A Type II report goes further and tests whether those controls actually operated effectively over a review period, proving the controls weren't just written down but were genuinely running — which is exactly what makes it the one serious enterprise buyers ask for.

questions.prompt: Match each compliance tool from Lesson 27 to what it actually does.
right: Continuously collects evidence against a prebuilt framework, pulled automatically from sources like AWS Config and CloudTrail
A deployable collection of Config rules, and optional remediation, evaluating resources against an entire framework at once
Scores an environment against a chosen framework and lists specific technical and non-technical improvement actions
A built-in bundle of policy definitions mapped to a named framework, feeding the Defender for Cloud compliance dashboard
questions.explain: Purview Compliance Manager scores an environment and lists specific, named gaps, both technical and non-technical. Azure Policy's regulatory compliance initiatives are what actually feed the Defender for Cloud compliance dashboard from Chapter 5. AWS Audit Manager continuously gathers evidence ahead of a real audit instead of scrambling for it during one. A Config conformance pack bundles an entire framework's worth of checks into one deployable unit.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is relying on a cloud provider's own independently audited controls, such as its SOC 2 report, to satisfy the infrastructure portion of your own compliance audit, treating the provider as a sub-service organization.
questions.explain: Compliance inheritance is the legitimate shortcut that lets your own auditor accept AWS's or Azure's audited report as proof for the infrastructure layer, instead of re-testing the provider's physical security themselves — but it only ever covers that layer, never the access controls and configuration decisions that remain entirely your own audit scope.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 30's Caldwell Logistics lab, why can Key Vault automatically rotate the customer-managed key protecting caldwelldocsstorage on a schedule, but not the OrderDbConnection secret the same way?
options: Key Vault can generate a new version of a key itself, but it has no way to generate a new database password on its own — it can only flag the secret's approaching expiration and let an Azure Function finish the rotation
Secrets are always less sensitive than keys, so Key Vault doesn't bother rotating them automatically
The customer-managed key has soft-delete and purge protection enabled, while the secret does not, and that is what blocks automatic secret rotation
Database connection strings can never be stored as Key Vault secrets, only as keys
questions.explain: A Key Vault key, like Caldwell's CMK, supports an automatic rotation policy because Key Vault itself can generate new key material. A secret like a database connection string is different — Key Vault has no way to know how to generate a new database password, so it can only set an expiration date and fire a notification as it approaches, which Caldwell's team wires to an Azure Function that actually performs the rotation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Caldwell Logistics' CSPM remediation case study in Lesson 31.
options: The account-level AllowBlobPublicAccess setting is the real kill switch — once it's off, no container on that account can be public regardless of its own setting
The team ran both the account-level and container-level remediation commands, even though the account-level one alone would have closed the exposure
Diagnostic logs showed anonymous GET requests from unknown IPs well beyond the auditor's own range, confirming the data had actually been exploited by outsiders
Caldwell's team added an Azure Policy with a deny effect so allowBlobPublicAccess can't be turned back on, even by accident
The team waited for Defender for Cloud's next automatic refresh cycle instead of forcing a fresh assessment
questions.explain: The account-level setting is confirmed as the real kill switch, and the team ran both the account-level and container-level commands anyway, so the container's own setting is also clean if anyone checks it directly later. An Azure Policy with a deny effect was added to prevent a repeat. The diagnostic logs showed only hits from the auditor's known IP range and nothing else suspicious, not evidence of outside exploitation, and the team forced a fresh assessment from the recommendation's details page rather than waiting on the automatic refresh cycle.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 31, instead of making a container public again for a one-off external share, Caldwell's team documented generating a time-limited, scoped ________ for sharing just one blob.
questions.explain: A SAS token is a time-limited, scoped credential for sharing one object without making anything publicly accessible — exactly the documented alternative Caldwell's team put in place for the next time someone outside the company needs a file, instead of repeating the contractor's public-access shortcut.
